idiom_name: continuity class + NavigableMap<LocalDate, Version> (TreeMap) with floorEntry as-of lookup
implementation_notes: Fowler's temporal collection is exactly a NavigableMap: the continuity owns a TreeMap keyed by the effective java.time.LocalDate, current() is lastEntry() and asOf(date) is floorEntry(date), so no search code is hand-written - only the two roles are. Versions should be immutable (the record shown here needs Java 16+; on Java 8 use final fields with no setters): an amendment copies the version in force, changes the copy and puts it at its effective date, which keeps published states frozen. The persisted form of the same model is a version table keyed by (identity, effective_date) with no separate continuity row, which is what JPA maps to; Hibernate Envers supplies that store together with an as-of query API (second variant).
pitfalls: floorEntry returns the greatest key <= date while lowerEntry/higherEntry shift by one version - the boundary rule must live in one method, especially when the query date equals an effective date.
Sharing a mutable Version instance between the map and callers lets a later edit rewrite history; use a record or final fields and defensive copies of collections.
TreeMap needs a consistent comparator and LocalDate carries no time zone: switching keys to Instant/LocalDateTime or mixing calendar systems breaks the assumption that one key is one resolvable day.

JPA entity identity: a version class annotated as an @Entity gets its own id and lifecycle, so the continuity/version split must survive proxies, equals/hashCode and lazy loading - never let the ORM merge a published version over the current one.

variants.name: Hibernate Envers audited entity with AuditReader as-of queries
variants.implementation_notes: Envers is the framework realization: annotate the entity with @Audited and Hibernate maintains audit tables plus a revision entity, one revision per transaction; AuditReader.find(Contract.class, id, date) returns the entity state current at a date and getRevisionNumberForDate(date) maps a date to its revision, with getRevisions listing when an entity changed. That is record-time versioning (what the row was at each commit), so it satisfies audit and 'as we knew it then' reads, while effective-date amendments still need their own column and query. Choose it when the stack is already Hibernate/JPA and the requirement is history of entity state rather than a business-named amendment object.
pitfalls: Audit rows accumulate for every audited entity and transaction; the audit tables need their own retention, indexing and purge policy.
find returns null for states where the entity did not exist yet and deleted entities are excluded unless includeDeletions is requested, so as-of reads must handle absence explicitly.
Enabling @Audited later does not backfill history - revisions start when auditing is switched on, so the first revision has no predecessor.
Audited relations resolve to the current target when the target is not audited (targetAuditMode), which silently mixes times inside an otherwise historical read.
